headline: Kyrgyz pay up 29.4% to about 5,330 Iradi som; ISEZ's last average was 3,250
dek: The ISEZ has published no 2026 average wage, and the Ministry of Economy repeats that public pay is set in som and paid in som, with no indexation announced.
paragraphs: Average pay in Kyrgyzstan from January to September 2026 reached 55,525 Kyrgyz soms a month, 29.4% more than in the same months of 2025, according to Kyrgyz statistics reported on Monday. At the Bank of Irad's official cross rate of 100 Kyrgyz soms to 9.6 Iradi som, that is about 5,330 Iradi som a month.

The latest comparable figure for the Irad Special Economic Zone is the 2025 average of 3,250 som a month, published by the Territorial Statistics Office in its quarterly bulletin *Wages and Incomes*. The office has issued no 2026 average. The Kyrgyz figure is therefore about 64% above the ISEZ's last published one, though the two cover different periods.

The gap looks wider in dollars. At the official 8.40 per dollar, 5,330 som is about US$634 and 3,250 som is about US$387. At the Bazar-i Kalan changers' sell rate this morning, 11.90 (buy 11.55), the ISEZ average buys about US$273. Consumer prices rose 7.9% in the year to September, the Territorial Statistics Office's latest reading.

The comparison is rough, and Prof. Raisa Akmatova, an economist at Talas State University, said so. "These are nominal figures for different periods, and Kyrgyz pay started from a different base and a different basket of prices," she said. "A 29.4% rise tells us how fast pay grew there. It does not tell us how much a family can buy in Jalal-Abad or in Talas." She said a fair comparison would need real wages and the 2026 ISEZ series, which does not yet exist.

Bekbolot Sherov, press secretary of the Ministry of Economy, repeated the ministry's standing position when asked whether the Kyrgyz figures would change it. "Wages in the Zone are set in som and paid in som," he said. He did not say when a 2026 average would be published, and said no indexation of public pay had been announced.

That is the sore point for public-sector staff, whose pay is fixed in som at 8.40 while rents, cars and imports follow the dollar. Rahat Osmon kyzy, chair of the Teachers' and Educators' Union, which has about 38,000 members, said the Kyrgyz numbers support the request her union made in June for pay indexed to the street rate. "A teacher in Talas does not ask what the budget calls a som," she said. The average teacher's pay was about 2,300 som in 2025, against 1,040 som for the Statistics Office's subsistence minimum for a working-age adult in the third quarter.

In the Bazar-i Kalan, Mairam Ergeshova, 62, who trades in dry goods in row 6, said her cousins across the Kyrgyz frontier had been telling her about their pay for a year. "They say wages went up and prices went up too, so it is not a holiday," she said. "But when the price of everything here follows the dollar and my neighbour's pension does not, I can do that sum myself." She said customers now ask for smaller portions of rice and flour.

The subject is not new. IradOne reported on Thursday that Bishkek had amended its labour code on wage indexing, and the Nurzhan weekly *Vecherniy Nurzhan* reported on Friday on what that meant for pay here. The Herald has also reported the squeeze on teachers, nurses and pensioners, whose average old-age pension was 1,250 som in 2025.

The next opening for an answer is the 2027 budget. The Ministry of Economy drafts it, the Governor's office sends it to the Mejlis this month and it normally passes in December. Only a summary is published, so whether it contains any provision for public pay will not be clear from the figures the public sees.
